routes.fa: Sam Boyce, Lani Chapko, Kyle Willis, 2020 (reconnaissance trip June 2020; completed capsule-style on a send push of roughly 7 days of climbing, late July-August 2020)

routes.overview: Jötnar is the most sustained aid route in Washington State, ascending the left side of Mount Index's North Norwegian Buttress via a continuous crack system located approximately 100 yards left of the Doorish line. The route features 2,000 feet of mixed free and aid climbing across 16 pitches on granite with strong alpine ambiance.
routes.beta: This is the only repeatable Grade VI big wall in the Pacific Northwest with bolted stainless steel anchors and portaledge bivy opportunities achievable by experienced wall climbers in 3-4 days. Climbing follows a continuous crack system featuring varied aid pitches including thin pins, rivets, hooks, and roof passages. The Fang Roof (Pitch 8) stands out as a classic pitch with hand crack free climbing through an overhang. Plan for 7 days of capsule-style climbing with portaledge camps to complete the first ascent.
routes.turnaround: Alpine big wall climbing requires deliberate early turnaround decisions. If bivy sites are not established by mid-afternoon on each climbing day, or if weather deteriorates significantly, retreat using existing rappel anchors. Descent takes 12+ hours and must be completed safely; do not push to summit under marginal conditions.
routes.rappels: Rappel the route (~16 raps from bolted anchors on all pitches but P15); much of the wall overhangs, so many rappels swing significantly or need a directional piece left to reach the next station cleanly; expect to down-aid a long section of P7 if no fixed line was left in place
routes.permit: No wilderness permit applies - the Lake Serene trailhead is south of US-2 on Mt. Index Road, outside the Wild Sky Wilderness, which lies north of the highway. A recreation pass is required for day use.
routes.comms: Cell phone coverage is limited and unreliable in the cirque and on the wall due to terrain and lack of tower infrastructure. Satellite communication options (satellite messengers, InReach, or Globalstar devices) are strongly recommended for emergency contact and trip coordination on multiday climbs.
routes.descent: Rappel the entire route. Many pitches overhang significantly; use directional gear placements for anchor setup. Pitch 7 requires either fixed lines or down-aiding (pitch overhangs 40+ feet). First ascensionists used one climber riding haul bags down approximately 1,000-1,200 feet before final team double-rope rappels off route anchors. Minimize environmental impact by removing all fixed lines.
obj_haz: rockfall from North Index and the buttress-Middle Index gully (worst in early-season snowmelt)

routes.detailed_rack: Climbers should bring a double rack of nuts and cams ranging from micronuts to #4 Camalots with one #5 Camalot. Include a single set of offset cams, 5 each of beaks in various sizes, 2 lost arrows for aid placement, and 10 rivet hangers (some in #1 size for deeper rivets). Two sets of hooks are essential given the blank sections requiring creative aid placements. A quality portaledge with fly and rain shell is non-negotiable, as afternoon seepage creates waterfall conditions on pitches 5-6. The route features bolted anchors, but climbers should verify anchor condition before committing full body weight and be prepared for occasional loose bolts.

Plan portaledge bivy sites carefully; only sheltered slabby belay ledges exist on Pitches 3 and 9, so other nights require suspended sleeping

Afternoon seepage on Pitches 5-6 creates waterfall conditions; start early and try to pass these pitches before midday if possible

Dehydration is a real risk on multiday climbs due to sustained effort and limited water access; drink consistently and plan water management carefully
Winter climbing is dangerous here due to wet avalanche danger and waterfall ice; avoid November through June
The descent demands serious rope management and anchor skill; an error here is far more dangerous than climbing
routes.pro_needs: Protection is a mix of aid placements and bolted anchors. Lower pitches rely on crack climbing with natural protection (nuts and cams), while upper pitches require rivet placements, hooks, and beaks on blank sections. The route features some bolted anchors already in place from the first ascent, but climbers must assess anchor condition, bring spares for critical bivy sites, and be prepared for creative placements on sections lacking traditional cracks.
routes.best_season: Late July through early September is the optimal climbing window, chosen specifically to avoid the spring and early summer snowmelt that creates seasonal waterfalls on pitches 5-6. The marine west coast climate brings wet, heavy snow in winter with high avalanche danger, making winter climbing inadvisable. Summer offers the most stable weather and lowest objective hazards.
routes.approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, hike Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then follow the unofficial path around the right-hand (west) side of the lake and traverse talus and huge boulders toward its south end below the Middle Peak (Jötunheim) massif. This cirque holds the Norwegian Buttresses, home to big-wall routes like Jötnar, one of the tallest walls in the Lower 48; reaching the base involves further talus and brush travel beyond the lake. Given the technical, multi-day nature of routes here, most parties approach with overnight gear.
routes.descent_text: The descent is accomplished by rappelling the route in full. Due to the sustained overhanging terrain throughout most pitches, careful anchor placement is critical, particularly on pitches with significant roofs. Climbers should plan to use at least two ropes for rappelling. The first ascent team used an unconventional technique where one climber managed haul bags on a very long rappel before the remaining climbers rappelled in pairs off stainless steel anchors. Plan to remove fixed lines during descent to preserve the rock.
routes.bail: There is no quick walk-off below the mid-height ledge system (~pitch 10); retreat means rappelling the route on its bolted anchors (natural gear needed at pitch 15). Carry a dedicated rap kit and be prepared to leave gear/fixed lines if bailing before anchors are established on a given pitch.

routes.itinerary: Day 1: Hike Lake Serene trail (4.1 miles, 2000 ft gain, 2-2.5 hours), approach cirque (30 min), scout wall and bivy location (1-2 hours). Day 2-5: Climbing days with portaledge camps. First ascensionists climbed Pitches 1-3 with bivy on Pitch 3. Pitch 4 (crux A3+) and Pitch 8 (Fang Roof) are highlights. Days 6-7: Finish upper pitches to summit, then full rappel descent (10-12 hours). Multiday success requires disciplined pacing and weather monitoring.

July.reason: The wall dries through the month; early July can still have wet cracks, so late July gives the best chance of dry pitches.

June.reason: Snowmelt runs as waterfalls down pitches 5-6 and the north-facing wall stays wet, mossy and dripping, with loose rock in the water paths.

August.reason: The driest pitches and the most stable multi-day weather for a 3-4 day wall; hot spells make water supply on the wall critical.

October.reason: Autumn rain re-wets the cracks and returns the seasonal waterfalls, and storms make a multi-day wall commitment dangerous.

September.reason: Early September usually stays dry, but shortening days and the return of autumn rain soon soak the wall again.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene talus to the left side of the buttress
approach_variants.notes: Maintained trail to Lake Serene, then the short unofficial path around the right-hand (west) side of the lake, down granite slabs to the talus fan and up the talus to the wall. Fill water at the lake; there is none above it. In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow. With haul bags and a multi-day load this takes considerably longer than the mileage implies, and the last of it is steepening mossy slab and brush that parties commonly rope up for before they reach clean rock.
hazards: Natural rockfall off North Index and out of the cleft between this buttress and Middle Index
Seasonal waterfalls running the lower pitches in spring and early summer
Loose and vegetated rock at the base and below the sixth pitch
Wet granite slabs on the lakeside traverse
A sustained overhanging wall with no walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is on the left side of the buttress, about a hundred yards left of the Doorish line, in a crack system that runs continuously from the ground. That continuity is the tell — the neighbouring weaknesses on this side peter out within a couple of hundred feet, so if the crack you are looking at closes above you, you are not on it. Use the Doorish line as your reference and count leftward from it rather than trying to identify the start in isolation; from the talus the whole left flank looks alike. Do not sort gear at the foot of the wall: the base is a rockfall alley fed by North Index above and by the deep cleft between this buttress and Middle Index, so stay low near the lake to rack up and keep time directly beneath the face as short as you can. Below the clean granite is a band of steepening mossy slab and brush that is part of the approach rather than part of the route, and roping up for it is normal rather than timid.

bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
bivy.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, on slab and talus. That spot sits close to the edge of the quarter-mile no-camping ring, probably just outside it but not by a comfortable margin, so sleep as high and as far from the shore as the ground allows and be ready to move if asked. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

routes.overview: The North Norwegian Buttress is a roughly 2,000-foot buttress on Mount Index's northeast face, plainly visible from US 2 above Lake Serene. A deep cleft between the Main and Middle summits separates it from the smaller South Norwegian Buttress. For decades it saw almost no traffic: a 1980s solo aid line and the 2002 Voodoo Project were its only routes, and neither has been repeated. Jötnar (VI 5.9 A3+, 16 pitches) was climbed in 2020 capsule-style over two trips and 14 days. This page describes Jötnar. The bolted free line Bluebell (5.13-), freed in 2023, is a separate route on the same buttress.
routes.beta: Jötnar follows a continuous crack system on the left side of the North Norwegian Buttress, roughly 100 yards left of the original 1980s aid line. It is a 16-pitch big wall at VI 5.9 A3+, mostly aid: thin pins, beaks, hooks and rivets, with free sections up to 5.9+. The two aid cruxes are P4 (A3+) and P9 (A3). Natural ledges are few, so a portaledge is required. The tops of P3 and P6 make good ledge camps. Every belay is bolted stainless steel except P15, which is a gear belay. Climb it late July to early September. Before that, snowmelt turns P5 and P6 into a waterfall in the afternoon, so climb them in the morning. Rack: double set of nuts and cams from micronuts to a #4 Camalot plus one #5, a set of offsets, 5 beaks, 2 Lost Arrows, 10 rivet hangers (some rivets are deep and need the #1 size), 2 sets of hooks, and a ledge fly and rain shell for the middle of the wall.
routes.turnaround: Set a conservative turnaround; retreat is complex on this committing face.
routes.rappels: Rappel the route from its bolted stainless anchors. P15 is the one gear belay, and its bolted rappel anchor is at the far right of that ledge. Overhanging pitches need swings or directionals, and P7 needs a fixed line or down-aiding.
routes.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: No cell service at elevation. Satellite communicator (InReach, Spot) strongly recommended for multi-day wall climb.
routes.descent: Rappel the route itself off the bolted belays; there is no walk-off. The overhanging lower wall means swings between stations, and haul bags can be lowered a long way because there is little for them to snag on.
obj_haz: Rockfall off North Index and the gully between the buttress and Middle Index
Loose, chossy wide cracks on the aid lines
Seasonal waterfall/water flow low on the route
Long, committing retreat once established above the first few pitches

waypoints.note: Toe of the buttress above the head of the lake. A band of steepening mossy slab and brush leads to the clean rock where the pitches start. Stonefall comes down the cleft between the Main and Middle summits, so keep time under the wall short.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the lake and follow the climbers' path around the west shore over talus and large boulders, then work up the talus fan to the toe of the wall. In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and old snow.

sectionBreakdown.note: Hike the Lake Serene trail then leave it to traverse brushy talus and a steep gully system toward the toe of the North Norwegian Buttress; camp near the base to have a fresh start …

Rack up and start up the buttress at first light; Jötnar's 16 pitches are sustained aid, with wet, seepy pitches low down. Climb to a portaledge camp (sites at pitches 3, 6 and 12) rather than trying to top out the same day.
Finish the remaining pitches, then rappel the route off its bolted belays and hike out; expect overhanging rappels that need swings.

routes.detailed_rack: Comprehensive rack: cams to large, full set of nuts, some aid gear and possibly pitons for the harder/looser sections.
pro_tips: Expect loose and vegetated rock — Index is not clean granite.
The approach and descent are as serious as the climbing.
Go light but bring enough to handle aid and loose terrain.
routes.pro_needs: Double rack from micronuts to a #4 Camalot plus a single #5, offsets, beaks, lost arrows and rivet hangers for aid to A3+; the belays are bolted except the 15th.
routes.best_season: Mid to late summer when the rock and brush are driest.
routes.approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail — roughly 3.6-4.1 miles (accounts vary slightly) and about 2,000 ft of gain, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur around mile 1.6 and switchbacking up to Lake Serene (~2,600 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail for the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders around the west side of the lake; in early summer this crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice at the lake's edge. Continue up talus beneath the imposing north/east face of North Index toward the cirque below the Norwegian Buttresses, then work up through the brushy base of the wall — steepening mossy slabs and brush that some parties rope up for before reaching clean rock on the buttress proper. Reliable water is available at Lake Serene and its outlet creek, but not higher on the talus approach, so fill up at the lake. Plan roughly 2-3 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, more with a loaded pack for a multi-day ascent.
routes.descent_text: Descend by rappelling Jötnar from its bolted stations. There is no walk-off. Many pitches overhang, so expect to swing in or clip directional gear to reach the next anchor. P7 overhangs more than 40 ft: leave a fixed line on it during the ascent, or be ready to down-aid it on the way down. P15's climbing belay is on gear, and its bolted rappel anchor sits at the far right end of the same ledge. Strip every fixed line as you go rather than leaving it on the wall. From the base, reverse the talus traverse around Lake Serene to the maintained trail.
routes.bail: Retreat is involved on the steep buttress; commit only with experience and good conditions.

pitch_detail.notes: Wandering, poorly protected face climbing (5.7 R) up to the huge right-trending ramp system visible from Lake Serene. Where it starts depends on the snowpack. On the first ascent it began a couple of hundred metres right of the main watercourse, out of a shallow moat. Belay at a bolted anchor.

Easy free climbing up a small ramp, then steep cracks and thin aid on the face below a splitter, finishing on a large ledge. Much of the original A4 R section has deteriorated. This pitch can be linked with P3.
Clean splitter cracks to a sheltered, slabby belay. The belay is a good portaledge site, sheltered from above.

The aid crux. Climb an A3 left-facing crack with a roof halfway up. Hook out under the loose-looking roof block to reach a crack that takes beaks well, then exit right on hooks to a stance below the muddy corner.
A left-facing corner below a slab. Snowmelt turns it into a waterfall from the afternoon on, so aim to be on it early in the morning. Linking it with P6 is recommended.
Easy slab, then a thin seam and A2 face climbing with a lot of hooking to the belay, which makes an excellent portaledge bivy.
Rivets up a left-facing corner lead into wildly steep cracks. The pitch overhangs more than 40 ft, so fix a line here for the descent, or plan to down-aid it. A 40 m rope reaches the next belay.

The Fang Roof. Start on A2, then take a beautiful splitter hand crack out through the overhang. It is aided at C1 here, though it would go free at about 5.10. Exit with 5.9 free climbing to the belay.

The second aid crux. Go right of the vegetation and aid up on thin pins, rivets and many hooks. A long bat-hook section avoids a chossy corner. Near the top, at a bolt, either tension traverse right or make a big reach to beak placements.
Follow a shallow right-facing flake trending left beneath a huge hanging roof and arête. Tension traverse left using hooks and short free sections to the belay.
Pass a bolt into a crack and follow it to its end, then easy free climbing to a good grassy ledge.

The Headwall. Free climb (5.8) straight up to a bolt, traverse right into a chimney hole, and hook out of a roof on hooks and rivets. Tricky beaks lead to a long rivet ladder with occasional free moves. Avoid hauling above this pitch if you can.
Free climbing off the belay on thin gear, then trend left along a crack past a short rivet ladder and a false belay. Weave back right to a good ledge on the crest of the buttress.
Runout face climbing straight off the belay through broken ledges near the buttress crest. Two trees guard the belay, and the climbing stays close to the crest.

Traverse a long way left to a large right-facing corner. Free it at about 5.10 or aid it at C1 on roots, then grovel through cedars to a large ledge. The only gear belay on the route takes finger to hand sizes. The bolted rappel anchor is at the far right end of this ledge.
A mossy 5.7 dihedral and a gully lead to the top of the buttress.

itinerary.cal: Best conditions are mid-to-late summer (Jul-Aug) once the approach brush and gully snow/ice have melted out and the wall has dried from spring seepage.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Difficult and lengthy — a notoriously difficult approach/descent; plan for a very long, physically demanding day well beyond the roped climbing itself, and on a multi-day ascent the walk in is usually a day of its own with a loaded pack.

team efficiency for a very long alpine day
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Advanced/expert alpine rock climber. Grade VI commitment on notoriously loose, vegetated rock demands prior experience on serious, remote alpine routes and strong judgment about when to retreat.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-to-late July through August, when the rock and brush are driest.

July.reason: Drying out; a solid month, though brush and rock are rarely fully dry.

June.reason: Early season conditions (wet, snowy up high, heavy brush) often persist into June on this west-slope peak.

August.reason: Driest window of the season for both rock and brush.

September.reason: Wet weather begins returning and rock turns greasy, compounding the already loose/vegetated character of the route.

weather.typical: Wet west-slope environment; rock and brush are rarely fully dry even in the best months (.typical).
weather.probability: Lower afternoon-thunderstorm frequency than the drier east-side Cascades; primary risk is fast-moving Pacific frontal systems bringing rain with little warning.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High-consequence exposure throughout a sustained Grade VI buttress; loose and vegetated rock raises both fall risk and rockfall risk onto the party, and retreat is committing once underway.

routes.rappel_count_note: Rappel the route, one rappel per pitch: every pitch has a bolted stainless-steel anchor except pitch 15, whose gear belay has a bolted rappel anchor along the ledge to the right. Pitch lengths are not published, so no rappel lengths are given; bring two ropes. Much of the wall overhangs, so plan on directional pieces or swinging in to reach stations, and on fixing or down-aiding pitch 7. The first-ascent party descended unconventionally, one climber riding the haul bags down roughly 1,000-1,200 ft before the rest finished with double-rope rappels, which is not a plan for a repeat.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene to the foot of the buttress
approach_variants.notes: Maintained trail to Lake Serene past the Bridal Veil Falls spur, then the unofficial climbers' path around the right-hand (west) shore over talus and large boulders, down granite slabs, and up the talus fan to the wall. Fill water at the lake — there is none above it. In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow at the water's edge. Two to three hours from the car with a light pack, appreciably more with a loaded haul bag for a multi-day ascent.
hazards: Large natural rockfall off North Index and out of the cleft beside Middle Index
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early summer
Steepening mossy slabs and brush at the base that parties rope up for
Loose and vegetated rock low on the wall
No walk-off — every retreat from the buttress is by rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identify the wall before committing to any line on it. The North Norwegian Buttress is the roughly 2,000-foot face on Mount Index's northwest side rising directly above the head of the lake, and it is separated from the smaller South Norwegian Buttress by a deep cleft running up between the Main and Middle summits. That cleft is the boundary between the two buttresses and it is also the chute that funnels stonefall onto the approach, so work up the talus fan to the toe rather than traversing in high across the base. The bottom of the buttress is not the bottom of the climbing: below the clean granite lies a band of steepening mossy slab and brush, and the change from vegetated slab to continuous rock is where the pitches actually begin. Across the face the routes are located by counting off the Doorish line, the original aid line up the buttress, so find that first and work from it. Rack up low, near the lake, and keep your time directly beneath the wall short.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, on slab and talus. That spot sits close to the edge of the quarter-mile no-camping ring, probably just outside it but not by a comfortable margin, so sleep as high and as far from the shore as the ground allows and be ready to move if asked. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
bivy.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

routes.name: Tepeh Towers
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach
Loose rock near the summit
routes.overview: A very short, easy alpine rock add-on to an Eldorado Peak trip: one low-5th-class pitch and some scrambling to a minor summit visible across the icecap from camp.
routes.beta: Climbed almost exclusively as a quick side objective from Eldorado's East Ridge camp — glacier travel to the base, a moat crossing, one short low-5th pitch, then scrambling to the top; round trip from camp is well under 2 hours.
routes.turnaround: Because the objective itself is short, the real time constraint is glacier travel to and from camp — turn back toward camp with enough daylight margin to recross the moat and any softening snow bridges before conditions deteriorate.
routes.rappels: 1 rappel below the summit back to the glacier
routes.comms: Cell service is unreliable to absent in the Inspiration Glacier basin; carry a satellite communicator or PLB for emergencies.
obj_haz: Moat crossing at the rock/ice interface

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH
waypoints.directions: From Seattle, take I-5 north then follow WA-20, the North Cascades Highway, east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit; reserve in advance on Recreation.gov or pick up a limited walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp
waypoints.directions: Walk back a short way along the road to the current crossing of the Cascade River, a log or a braided ford that shifts year to year, then climb the steep unmaintained climbers' path through old growth to a boulder field, cross Eldorado Creek and continue into the Eldorado Creek basin meadows. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier to the camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet.

waypoints.name: Base of Tepeh Towers
waypoints.note: ~45 min glacier walk N/NW from camp to where the towers rise off the Eldorado ice cap.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and walk the glacier north-northwest for about 45 minutes to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arete that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: Tepeh Towers
waypoints.note: One short low-5th-class pitch above the moat, then a scramble to the top.
waypoints.directions: Climb high on the glacier to where it rests against the rock and cross the moat. One short low-fifth-class pitch, then easy scrambling, leads to the summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Morning, after arriving at Eldorado high camp

routes.detailed_rack: A single light rack to 2 inches plus a handful of slings is enough for the one short pitch; the rest is glacier and scrambling gear.
pro_tips: Combine with Eldorado's East Ridge, Klawatti Peak, and/or Austera Peak from the same high camp to make the most of the approach effort
watch_out: Moat width and difficulty change through the season — assess before committing to the crossing
routes.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed — one short low-5th pitch with a small rack.
routes.best_season: Best once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower opens enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late season; most parties combine it with an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse in July or August.
routes.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) up the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. From the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600 ft), rope up and walk about 45 minutes north-northwest across the glacier to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arête that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.
routes.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb or rappel from a fixed rappel station directly below the top, landing back on the glacier for the return traverse to camp.
routes.bail: The route is short enough that retreat is simply reversing the line at any point; the main constraint is the glacier moat crossing, which can become harder to reverse as the day warms.

pitch_detail.notes: About 45 minutes north-northwest of the Eldorado East Ridge camp: climb high on the glacier to where it meets the rock and cross the moat onto the tower. Roped glacier travel; bring crampons, axe and pickets.
One short, low fifth-class pitch off the moat. A single rack to 2 in and slings for the anchor are enough.
Easy scrambling above the pitch to the top. Return by downclimbing, or rappel from the fixed station just below the summit back onto the glacier (bring a 60 m rope).

routes.itinerary: Day 1: approach to Eldorado high camp (~7,600 ft) via Eldorado Creek and Eldorado Glacier. Day 2: ~45 min glacier approach north/northwest to Tepeh Towers, climb the short route (~30 min), return to camp or continue on to Austera Peak. Day 3: hike out.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass ($5/day equivalent) for trailhead parking; the wilderness permit itself is free to obtain in person at Marblemount, though Recreation.gov charges a small fee for advance-reserved permits
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the Mount Shuksan, Eldorado Peak and Forbidden Peak cross-country zones, which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry wilderness permit required for camping, issued by the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount for the Inspiration zone
access.closures: Cascade River Road is gated and closed to vehicles in winter; check NPS road-conditions page for current washout/closure status
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS) / Stephen Mather Wilderness
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass at the Eldorado Creek Trailhead

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount; $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee.

road.name: Cascade River Road (from Marblemount) to Boston Basin/Eldorado trailhead area
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel with potholes and washboard; passenger cars can often reach mile ~18 (NP boundary) but a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for the final miles to the Eldorado TH/Boston Basin pulloff (~mile 20-21.7). Vulnerable to washouts/flooding closures, especially in spring and after heavy rain.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3-3.5 hours from Seattle to Marblemount, then 45 min-1+ hour further up Cascade River Road to the trailhead area.
road.seasonalGate: Only snow-cleared and opened each spring/early summer; check the NPS North Cascades road-conditions page before driving.

climate.fall: Glaciers exposed as bare/blue ice by September, requiring ice screws in places
climate.spring: Deep snowpack with well-bridged but hidden crevasses after fresh snowfall
climate.summer: Prime climbing season; approach trail largely snow-free by August, glacier travel remains necessary all season
climate.winter: Heavy snow, avalanche hazard, and a closed access road — essentially unclimbed this season
climate.typical: Cool, wet, and often cloudy; the Eldorado Icecap generates its own localized weather that can diverge sharply from valley forecasts

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent in the Eldorado Icecap basin; rescue response may take hours to days depending on weather and terrain
emergency.rangerStation: Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to mid-August, when the moat at the base of the rock has opened enough to cross but is not yet too wide

July.reason: The glacier is well bridged for the walk to the towers and the moat is usually crossable; the rock pitch dries out.

June.reason: Deep snow on the Eldorado approach and the glacier; the moat is often still buried, and the rock above it may hold snow.

August.reason: The rock is dry and the glacier is still mostly sealed, but the moat widens and crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier open toward late month.

October.reason: Early snow and cold on an exposed glacier camp, short days, and the Cascade River Road can be gated for winter.

September.reason: The moat can be wide and awkward and the glacier more crevassed; stable fall weather still makes it a quick side trip from camp.

approach_variants.name: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
approach_variants.notes: Everything below the ice cap is the standard Eldorado approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, backtrack a short way along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River (a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts year to year), then the steep unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,000-3,500 ft through old growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine meadows of Eldorado Creek basin — commonly five to six hours from the car. Push on to the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,600 ft. From that camp it is roughly a 45-minute roped glacier walk north-northwest to where the towers rise out of the icecap. The towers sit at the saddle you cross anyway to get from the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister — so most parties pass beneath them on the way to Klawatti, Austera or Dorado Needle and climb one as a side objective. Round trip from camp is well under two hours.
approach_variants.season: Once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower has opened enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late in the season — usually July or August, most often as part of an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach — roped travel and crevasse rescue gear, not an unroped stroll
The moat where the glacier rests against the rock, which is the whole gate on this climb
Loose rock near the summit
Softening snow bridges on the return, which is the real time constraint on such a short objective
approach_variants.baseFinding: Tepeh Towers is an arête of many spires, not one tower — that is the first thing to understand, and it is why the base finding here has to be about the moat rather than about the skyline. The formation is a rock arête poking out of the icecap northwest of the Inspiration Glacier, with Eldorado to the west and Klawatti to the northeast, and it carries a great many small spires. So the procedure is: climb high on the glacier until the ice is resting against the rock, and cross the moat there. You are looking for the point where the snow meets the rock cleanly enough to step across; that point, not a particular spire seen from a distance, is what you navigate to. The positive confirmation is fixed gear, and it is the only discriminator published for this formation: the Tower Parties climb has rappel anchors directly below its summit. If you top out and there is no anchor below you, you have climbed a neighbouring spire — which is not dangerous here, but it is not the recorded line either. The length test is short and unambiguous: one short low-fifth pitch above the moat, then scrambling to the top. If you are running out a second and third rope length, you are on something else on the same arête. What is honestly not known: no published account names which of the spires is the climbed one or gives a way to tell it from its neighbours at a distance. That gap is stated here rather than filled — treat the anchor below the summit as the confirmation and the moat as the navigation.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out
